definitions.definition: Rules in physics that say certain things (like energy or momentum) never change in total amount, even when they move or change form.
definitions.example: When you drop a ball, its energy changes from stored (potential) to moving (kinetic), but the total energy stays the same.

definitions.definition: Something that cannot be broken or disobeyed, no matter what.
definitions.example: The rule that you can't be in two places at once is inviolable.

definitions.definition: A property where something stays the same even when you change something about it, like rotating a circle or shifting time forward.
definitions.example: A snowflake looks the same when you rotate it 60 degrees.

definitions.definition: A famous math proof that every conservation law comes from a symmetry in nature.
definitions.example: Because the laws of physics are the same today as yesterday (time symmetry), energy is conserved.

definitions.definition: The idea that the laws of physics don't change from one moment to the next.
definitions.example: Gravity worked the same way yesterday as it does today.

definitions.definition: A basic assumption that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for other ideas.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A physical property (like energy or charge) that stays constant in a closed system over time.
definitions.example: The total electric charge in a sealed box never changes.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the Second Law of Thermodynamics says entropy always increases over time.
definitions.example: A messy room has higher entropy than a tidy one, and it naturally gets messier without effort.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why God Can't Look on Sin'

definitions.definition: The law of physics that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases or stays the same, never decreases.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts in a warm room because the system moves toward more disorder.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why God Can't Look on Sin'

definitions.definition: A physics framework that describes how particles (like electrons) are actually excitations in invisible fields that fill all of space.
definitions.example: An electron is like a ripple in an electron field that exists everywhere.

definitions.definition: A particle that carries a force between two other particles, allowing them to interact without touching.
definitions.example: A photon is the mediator that carries the electromagnetic force between two charged particles.

definitions.definition: A tiny particle of light that carries electromagnetic force and has no mass.
definitions.example: Light from a flashlight is made of billions of photons traveling at the speed of light.

definitions.definition: A particle that holds quarks together inside protons and neutrons by carrying the strong nuclear force.
definitions.example: Gluons are like the glue that keeps the parts of an atom's nucleus stuck together.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical particle that would carry the force of gravity, if gravity works like other quantum forces.
definitions.example: If gravitons exist, they would be like tiny messengers that tell matter to attract other matter.

definitions.definition: The Christian belief that God became a human being in the person of Jesus Christ.
definitions.example: Christmas celebrates the incarnation—God taking on a human body and life.

definitions.definition: Negative entropy; a measure of order or information that can be used to decrease disorder in a system.
definitions.example: Sunlight brings negentropy to Earth, allowing plants to grow and create order from chaos.

definitions.definition: Describing something that is not limited to a single point in space but can affect or exist in multiple places at once.
definitions.example: In quantum mechanics, two particles can be linked so that changing one instantly affects the other, even far away—that's nonlocal.

definitions.definition: Mathematical proofs showing that in any complex enough system, there are true statements that cannot be proven using the system's own rules.
definitions.example: No matter how many math rules you make, there will always be some true facts you can't prove with just those rules.

definitions.definition: A term from this framework meaning the limit that God's saving action must be infinite in duration to overcome the infinite gap between perfect order and finite disorder.
definitions.example: Just as you can't fill an infinite hole with a finite amount of dirt, salvation requires an infinite source.

definitions.definition: The process in quantum field theory where particles interact by exchanging other particles (like photons) that carry forces.
definitions.example: Two magnets repel each other by exchanging virtual photons between them.
